opus-5.5.text:
I think that ambition is understandable, but in my view it's not realistic to get there in one step, at least not in the way language models did.

Language models had a huge advantage: the internet had already accumulated trillions of tokens of text. The data existed before the model did. In embodied intelligence we don't have that. There's no "internet of robot actions." Every trajectory of a robot grasping, placing, or opening a drawer has to be collected, and real-world teleoperation data is extremely expensive and slow to scale. Even if you put thousands of robots into data collection, you're still orders of magnitude away from what language models trained on.

The second issue is that the physical world is much less forgiving. A language model that's right 90% of the time is already useful, because a human reads the output and corrects it. A robot that succeeds 90% of the time at a task, with failure meaning dropping something or knocking things over, is hard to deploy commercially. You need very high reliability, and generality and reliability pull against each other early on.

So my view is that the path has to be staged. First, use synthetic data and simulation at large scale to learn core skills like grasping, placing, and navigation, and get those to generalize across objects, scenes, and lighting. Then use a smaller amount of real-world data to align and close the sim-to-real gap. Then let the model go to real scenarios in specific verticals, such as retail, pharmacies, and factories, where it can create value, keep collecting data, and iterate. Through that loop, the skills accumulate and the model gradually becomes more general.

Generality is the destination, and I believe we will get there. But if you try to jump straight to a fully general embodied foundation model without solving data, reliability, and deployment, you risk building something impressive in demos that can't actually work in the real world. The key is finding a path where each step is commercially viable while you climb toward generality.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts the abundance of Internet text with the cost of collecting robot trajectories, but does not compare recorded visual data’s coverage of possible human visual observations with Internet text’s coverage of possible human language.

r002.rationale: The response says language models benefited from trillions of existing text tokens, but does not attribute their broad capabilities to training data covering the distribution of possible language.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll answer as the guest, He Wang, drawing only on the conversation so far.

I think the ambition is right, but "in one step" is where I'd push back. Language models got general because the data was already there: the whole internet, trillions of tokens, written by humans doing exactly the task we wanted the model to do. Embodied intelligence has nothing like that. There is no internet of robot actions. The data we have is fragmented across different robot bodies, different sensors, different labs, and most of it is small.

So when people say "let's do for robots what GPT did for text," I'd ask: what's the equivalent of the pretraining corpus? Right now the honest answer is that we're still building it. Some of it will come from teleoperation, some from simulation, some from human video, some from the robots themselves once they're deployed. That's a flywheel, not a single jump.

The second difference is that language is closed-loop with a human in the chair. If the model is wrong, a person reads it and corrects. A robot acts in the physical world, in real time, with contact and forces and consequences. Generalization there isn't just "can it describe a new object," it's "can it grasp an object it's never seen, in a kitchen it's never been in, without breaking something." That bar is much higher, and the failure modes are much more expensive.

My view is that we'll get there, but through layers. A model that generalizes across objects and scenes for a certain class of skills, like manipulation. Then across tasks. Then across embodiments. Each layer needs its own data and its own engineering. Anyone promising a fully general embodied model in one shot is either compressing a decade into a slide, or hasn't yet run a robot outside the lab for a week.

What I find exciting is that the foundation model mindset still applies. Large-scale pretraining, unified architectures, scaling laws. Those lessons transfer. It's the data supply and the physical grounding that don't come for free, and that's where the real work is.

r002.rationale: It attributes language models’ generality to training on the whole internet—trillions of tokens written by humans for the relevant task—clearly presenting that broad data supply as the reason for their capabilities.

astra-6.text:
I think that ambition is understandable, but expecting to get there in one step is unrealistic. Language models have a relatively unified interface: text goes in, text comes out. For an embodied model, you have to ask: general across which tasks, which environments, and which bodies? A capability learned on one robot may not transfer directly to another, because its sensors, joints, and ways of interacting with the world are different.

There’s also a feedback problem. Producing a plausible answer is one thing; taking an action that reliably achieves a physical goal is another. The robot has to observe what actually happened, correct its mistakes, and cope with changes in the environment.

So I would treat generality as a direction, and work toward it through concrete, measurable capabilities. Can the same model handle several tasks? Can it succeed in an unfamiliar setting? Can it transfer to a different robot with less additional training? Those are meaningful steps. We should be ambitious about the destination, but rigorous about what each step has actually demonstrated.

r001.rationale: The response discusses differences between language and embodied models, but does not compare the coverage of recorded visual data with Internet text.

r002.rationale: The response does not attribute language models’ broad capabilities to training data covering the distribution of possible language.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s a useful long-term ambition, but “in one step” is too optimistic. Language models operate through a relatively unified interface: text. An embodied model has to connect perception, decision-making, and physical action, and those actions depend on the robot’s body and its environment. A mistake also has a physical cost.

The key question is what we mean by generality. Does it mean handling new objects, performing new tasks, working in unfamiliar environments, or transferring across different robot bodies? Those are related, but progress on one doesn’t automatically solve the others.

I would pursue broad capabilities while making the milestones concrete. Can the system reliably complete a task? Can it adapt when conditions change? Can it recognize failure and recover? We need evidence on those questions before calling it general. The ambition can be large, but the path needs to be incremental.

r001.rationale: The response discusses embodied models and their challenges but does not compare recorded visual data coverage with Internet text coverage.
